title: How Long Does Pain Last After a Root Canal?
metaTitle: How Long Does Pain Last After a Root Canal?
metaDescription: How long tooth pain usually lasts after a root canal, what level of soreness is normal, and the warning signs that mean you should call your dentist.
secondaryKeywords: how long does root canal pain last
excerpt: Most soreness after a root canal fades within a few days. Here is what is normal, what is not, and when to reach out.
heroImageAlt: A calendar with a few days marked, representing the typical recovery period after a root canal.
bodyHtml:
For most people, mild to moderate soreness after a root canal lasts a few days and then gradually improves, with the first two to three days usually being the most noticeable. The discomfort is typically a dull ache or tenderness when biting, rather than the sharp or throbbing pain many people had before treatment. If pain is severe, lasts well beyond a week, or keeps getting worse instead of better, that is worth a call to your dentist.

Why a treated tooth can still feel sore

It can seem surprising that a tooth still aches after the nerve inside it has been removed. The soreness usually comes from the tissues and ligament around the root, not the pulp itself. These structures can be inflamed from the original infection and from the treatment, much like any part of the body feels tender for a short while after a procedure. The more inflamed or infected a tooth was beforehand, the more post-treatment tenderness tends to linger.

A typical timeline

Everyone heals differently, but a common pattern looks like this:

  • First 24 to 48 hours: the most tenderness, especially when chewing on that side; often eased by over-the-counter pain relief if your dentist agrees it is suitable for you.
  • Days three to seven: steady improvement, with the tooth feeling more normal each day.
  • After a week: most people have little or no discomfort, though a treated tooth can feel slightly different until the final restoration is placed and it fully settles.

This is a general guide, not a promise. Molars and teeth that had significant infection can take a little longer to calm down.

What is normal versus what is not

Expected, and usually fine: mild aching, tenderness when you tap or chew on the tooth, and some jaw soreness from keeping your mouth open during the appointment. Not expected, and worth prompt attention: pain that intensifies after the first few days, swelling of the gum or face, fever, a bad taste or discharge, or a reaction to medication. These do not necessarily mean something has gone wrong, but they should be assessed rather than ignored.

Easing the discomfort

Simple steps help most people through the first days. Over-the-counter pain relievers can be effective, but confirm what is appropriate for your health and other medications. Chew on the opposite side and favour softer foods while the tooth is tender. A cold compress on the cheek in short intervals can reduce discomfort, and a gentle warm salt-water rinse may feel soothing. Keep brushing and flossing normally, including around the treated tooth, since cleanliness supports healing. Getting enough rest in the first day or two also gives your body a chance to settle the inflammation, and many people find the tooth feels noticeably easier after a good night's sleep.

Is throbbing pain after a root canal a bad sign?

A little throbbing in the first day or two can occur as inflammation settles. Throbbing that builds over several days, wakes you at night, or comes with swelling is different and should be reported to your dentist.

Could a high bite be causing my pain?

Yes. If the filling or temporary sits even slightly high, the tooth takes extra force every time you bite, which keeps it sore. This is common and usually fixed quickly with a minor bite adjustment, so mention it if biting feels off.

Why might pain return weeks later?

Occasionally discomfort eases and then comes back. Reasons can include a bite issue, a tooth that needs its permanent restoration, or, less often, persistent infection that may need further treatment. Your dentist can examine the tooth and take an X-ray to find out.

When to seek care

Reach out promptly for worsening or severe pain, swelling, fever, or anything that feels clearly wrong. Finishing the recommended restoration also matters, because a tooth left with only a temporary filling is more prone to problems.
